newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota town struggles to hold back river.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota town struggles to hold back river.

text.p: Shouting encouragement over the roar of water pumps, residents of this farming community struggled Tuesday to shore up their leaking dike against the relentless rise of the Red River.

Sirens sounded and chaos erupted in the middle of the previous night when a crack in the dike was discovered and Drayton's 970 residents scrambled to heed an evacuation order. Among those returning to town to seal the gap and collect some possessions were lifelong Drayton resident Nick Rutherford and Deputy Sheriff Todd Schmiess.

"At least we've got everybody out of here so no one gets hurt if something happens," Schmiess said, recalling the death of a young motorist last spring when he was swept off a bridge by the river's swift current.

The town's six-mile-long dike stacked with snow-white sandbags wended through backyards and along garage walls, while gasoline-powered pumps sent fountains of water out of the city's still-functioning sewers back into the river. A city park, where Schmiess might fish for walleye and catfish in normal times, was invisible beneath stinking brown water.

The river overwhelmed the defences of Grand Forks 40 miles south over the weekend and was projected to rise another 3 feet at Drayton. Rutherford said he had never seen the river extend as far, casting his gaze toward Minnesota where the riverbank was unrecognizeable.

"It wasn't this high during the flood of 1979," he said. He stood atop the dike as he supervised a pair of small bulldozers shoving mounds of dirt near where the crack had formed. "We'll build it up. No choice, really."

Jim Young, a beet farmer from St. Thomas 13 miles to the west, arrived in a pickup truck with friends asking where they could lend a hand. The lucrative beet planting season was delayed by shallow ponds covering many fields and Drayton and other river towns have received volunteer help from all over.
"Yesterday we were here helping to evacuate people; the other day we were sandbagging," Young said.

St. Thomas, like several rural hamlets scattered across the flat prairie of the Red River valley, was swept by overland floodwaters from the massive spring melt, leaving behind a layer of silt on the streets that Tuesday's traffic lifted into dust clouds.
In Drayton, the enemy was water. Schmiess showed how his father Dennis' home was swamped up to the first floor even as a trickle of water seeped through the town's adjacent dike.

"If somebody's got a gun or is acting stupid, you can usually do something," Schmiess, who had not slept in two days, said. "If that river decides to come up, you can talk to it but that isn't going to help."
